newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Penang electronics makers brace for competition.
newsitem.headline: Penang electronics makers brace for competition.

text.p: Executives at Malaysia's Silicon Valley are busily examining ways of keeping Penang competitive in the face of a global electronics slowdown.
A group of about seven senior executives at Penang-based electronics firms have set up an informal group to discuss common problems and propose strategies for the future.

"(Do) we consider ourselves to be the best in the world, and if not, can we do something collectively?" Yap Peng Hooi, group member and managing director of Siemens Semiconductor Sdn Bhd, told Reuters.

The 'valley' executives say they are looking for ways to keep their manufacturing edge with wage escalation in Malaysia making the country less competitive against low-cost labour in Thailand, Vietnam, China and India.
Despite a global slowdown in the electronics industry, particularly among chip makers, which has dampened growth at some Penang firms, Malaysia has escaped relatively unscathed due to its diversity.

The popular resort island boasts almost 90 major electronics and electrical parts companies. Semiconductor makers account for some 40 percent but disk drives, audio equipment and personal computers are also manufactured.
The electronics and electrical industry accounts for about 60 percent of Penang's employment and about 50 percent of Malaysia's total exports.
With nearly 25 years experience in the industry, a trained workforce and relatively sound infrastructure, the northern island state has become a dominant manufacturing site.

Recently it welcomed PC maker Packard Bell, which cited lower operational costs and ease of expansion in choosing Penang for a new 300,000 square foot (28,000 square metre) plant over Singapore, Penang officials said.
But problems such as blackouts, including one in June 1995 which shut down the state's power-supply for 10 days, still require solutions.

The newly-formed executive think-tank aims to hold discussions every six weeks on issues which include productivity and skill-levels. Yap said the group hopes to eventually involve government in its efforts.
At present the joint government and private sector Penang Skills Development Centre provides technical, manufacturing and management training courses.
But even the executive director of the centre, Boonler Somchit, questioned if Penang and other northern states are producing enough skilled workers.

"At present, the situation is not serious enough to jeopardise our country as the government took short-term measures such as importing foreign workers," he said recently at an economic development conference.

Labour turnover in the industry is estimated at 48-60 percent annually, with yearly wage rises in the 10-15 percent range. But the job market is still strong. Some 3,600 workers recently laid off by Penang electronics firms were quickly snapped back up.
State agency Penang Development Corp (PDC) said it is not looking at many new applications for set-ups in its industrial parks, but about 15 existing tenants are looking to expand.
The five industrial parks in Penang occupy 5,850 acres (2,370 ha) and house over 700 factories.
"We have a very strong commitment to people who are here," said K. Gopalan, manager of the PDC's industry and trade division.
